lesson.title: The One-Way Flow: How Heat Moves From Hot to Cold
lesson.summary: Heat transfer is the movement of thermal energy from a warmer object to a cooler one until both reach the same temperature, and this chapter shows how to put a number on that flow.
lesson.body:
You already know that temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the particles in a sample, while heat is energy on the move. Heat is not a substance stored inside an object. It is energy in transit, and it only travels spontaneously in one direction: from a warmer object to a cooler one. Two objects placed in contact will exchange energy until they reach the same temperature, a condition called thermal equilibrium. A cold soda left on a counter never spontaneously gets colder while the room gets warmer. Energy always drains downhill, from high temperature to low temperature, the same way water flows downhill under gravity.

Heat travels by three mechanisms. Conduction is the transfer of energy through direct contact, as fast moving particles collide with slower moving neighbors and pass along kinetic energy, the way a metal spoon left in hot soup heats up along its whole length. Convection is the transfer of heat by the bulk movement of a fluid, such as warm water rising and cooler water sinking in a pot on a stove. Radiation is the transfer of energy by electromagnetic waves and needs no medium at all, which is how the sun warms the earth across empty space. In a chemistry lab, all three mechanisms are usually working against you at once, since heat you want to measure inside a calorimeter can conduct through its walls, drift off by convecting air currents, or radiate away, which is exactly why calorimeter design (covered soon) tries to minimize all three.

Because heat transfer obeys the law of conservation of energy, if two objects exchange heat and nothing escapes to the surroundings, the energy lost by the warmer object must exactly equal the energy gained by the cooler one. This single idea, heat lost equals heat gained, is the foundation of every calorimetry calculation you will do. To make heat transfer quantitative rather than just directional, chemists use the relationship q = m c delta T, where q is heat in joules, m is mass, delta T is the temperature change, and c is a property called specific heat capacity that you will define precisely in the next chapter. For now, treat c as a conversion factor that tells you how much energy a particular substance needs to absorb, or gives up, per gram per degree.

Here is a preview calculation using water, whose specific heat capacity is a well known value, c = 4.18 J/(g times degree C). Suppose 100.0 g of water is heated from 20.0 degrees C to 80.0 degrees C. The temperature change is delta T = 80.0 minus 20.0 = 60.0 degrees C. Applying q = m c delta T gives q = (100.0 g)(4.18 J/(g times degree C))(60.0 degrees C). Multiplying 100.0 by 4.18 gives 418 J per degree C, and multiplying that by 60.0 degrees C gives 25,080 J, or 25.1 kJ. That much energy had to flow into the water from somewhere hotter than the water, and by conservation of energy, whatever supplied that heat lost exactly 25.1 kJ. Notice the sign convention: q is positive here because the water absorbed energy. If you were tracking the heat source instead, its q would be negative, since it released the same amount of energy. Keeping careful track of these signs is essential once you start comparing what two objects in contact experience simultaneously, which is precisely the subject of calorimetry.
